Railroad, and railroad enterprises occupy a large share of the public attention, very naturally and justly, for they constitute the main avenues of the country's greatness and power—the chief promoters of the development of our wonderful resources—by shortening the distances between the producers and manufacturers and the great markets, and by throwing into comparative proximity different and distant communities. These advantages are well understood by most or all of our readers, and we allude to them more to call public attention to the present condition and prospects in railroad enterprises generally, than from any expectation of presenting anything new on the subject.

Time was when general fear possessed the public mind that railroad building had been overdone—that there had been already too many railroads completed, that the total ruin of many of them was a sure thing, and the idea of projecting others was deemed visionary and absurd. That time was not long ago. Little did men then seem to know and appreciate the extent of the country's resources.

A great change has taken place in the public mind in this regard, and the question now is, how shall we secure railroads enough to accommodate the vast amount of business that crowds with accommodating pressure. The means of transportation as an instance of this pressure we may state that no longer ago than last fall five hundred carloads of freight shipped from the West were lying immovable at Albany, because there was no transportation to take this large pile to the various points of its destination Eastward. A telegram was sent from Albany to Chicago, directing that no more freight be sent for places East of New York until further orders. Meanwhile people throughout New England were complaining of high prices caused in great measure by want of transportation. The total inadequacy of the railroads from Albany to Boston via Springfield and Worcester to meet the demand, and the unusual amount of freight thrown over the Vermont Central and the Rutland & Burlington, the last named road taking Western freight from the New York Central at Schenectady, are well known to railroad and other business men. It was proved that one of the best, if not the best of thoroughfares between Chicago and Boston was over the Rutland & Burlington road, connecting with the Cheshire and Fitchburg roads at Bellows Falls, and the New York Central and the roads farther West at Schenectady. Over this line, 900 barrels of apples were brought from the West in the short space of three weeks. The year 1854 was one memorable for the vast amount of business done by railroads, generally, and yet the Rutland & Burlington and Cheshire roads increased the business of each during the year of 1866 about 100,000. Considering the limited extent of these two roads this speaks well for their management. Indeed we doubt if there are better managed roads in the country. Active preparations are now being made to add greatly to the facilities of this line, the coming season, so that if there should be another blockade, such as existed last fall, it will not be the fault of the Rutland and Cheshire managers.

But the rapid expansion of railroads in the West—the probable completion of two Pacific lines as far as the fertile mineral regions of Colorado, within two or three years, and the crowded population that will be likely to gather there, will make a demand on Eastern roads mass is now little dreamed of.

No fears need be entertained that too many roads will be constructed in the East, so long as we can meet with roads leading from the West, so as to facilitate the means of transporting the increased millions of passengers and freight that will be moving between the Atlantic and Pacific shores.

The chartered line from Rutland to White River Junction will be wanted before many years, and the friends of that enterprise may as well be looking about for the ways and means for its construction.

We had intended to say something about the lines of railroad that are in rapid process of construction towards the Pacific, but time and space admonish us to postpone this branch of our subject to another day.

COLLOT the convention in Illuminations.

I have said that many of the principles
stated in the call are in my view unob-
jectionable. I will not stop to criticize
those which are objectionable, but con-

tent myself with stating that the call

fails to take any notice of one of the
great issues now before the American
people. I allude to the question wheth-

er the several States shall ratify or re-
ject the last amendment proposed by
Congress to the Constitution of the

United States. This is a grave and all

important question. The issue upon it

cannot be avoided. It should be placed

fairly and squarely before the people.

The failure to take ground upon so im-

portant and all-absorbing a question

must be attributed either to desire to

avoid the issue or as a declaration of be-

lief and policy against the adoption of

the amendment. Being myself earnest-

ly and decidedly in favor of the adoption

of the amendment by the States, I can-

not go into an organization that would

smother it by avoiding its discussion.

I must add that no man is more de-

sirous than am to attain the entire

restoration of the American Union, with

its practical workings in more perfect

harmony and concord than ever, and the

surety, as far as mortal affairs can be
made sure, of endless perpetuity in the
future. The blessings to flow from such
a Union are countless and inestimable,
but such union consistent within itself,
maintained by the universal con-
sent of all classes and sections and laugh-
ing to scorn both the assaults of foes
internal or external and the ravages of
time and change will only be obtained
by sternly retracting every departure
from or compromise with the su-
preme and general idea fundamental to
the American Constitution. That gen-
eral idea consists in brief of the politi-
cal liberty and equality of mankind un-
der the law. Such and such only can
be the Union, the nationality, that will
put in form the magnificent and lofty
dreams of the American continent in
mind and fulfill in the future the high-
est efforts of the presents and past. It is
not the vague delusion that the rights
of the States need doctoring. The Amer-
ican theory eliminates properly in the
sacredness of the rights of individuals
of each single individual. This after
all is what Washington carved out with
the sword and Jefferson filtering it thro'
his subtle and clear mind drew up and
put on record with the pen.

It is well known that in the practical
and logical history of the United States,
the only departures or compromises of
the kind alluded to have been those in
the interest of slavery and its manifold
incidents. I do not, of course, propose
to go over the thousand times told tale
of the past sixty years to-day; slavery,
as confessed legality, is as we all
know, no more; but some of the most
important of its incidents or compro-
misses still remain, blots and incongrui-
ties upon the law. What equitable rea-
son can be given why these incidents
also should not be erased? "Time was
when the brains were out the man would
die" but now we see the limbs demand-
ing to live and move, as if the nervous
centre still existed. The persistent at-
tempt to keep in the Constitution the
rule of an unequal and unfair basis of
representation is perilous to the future
peace of the country and will surely
cause a chafing sense of injustice as
long as it continues. Furthermore, the
high mission of the Union party, as
avowed in the Baltimore Convention
to extirpate slavery—includes the re-
moval of all the hateful and anti-popu-
lar excrescences engrafted by that insti-
tution for its own selfish aggrandize-
ment upon our free national laws and

tion cannot be accomplished until all
which slavery has so engrafted is cut
out, for until then slavery is not extir-

the men who look to a law of equal rep-
resentation as the only guarantee both

cence, I would feel myself out of place in

tation giving peculiar and unrighteous

Judging Of your future policy from the foreshadowings Of your able annual message TO the Thirty-ninth Congress, regarded myself (however humble) as one of your sincere friends and earnest supporters and looked upon you as the visible head and standard bearer OF the great Union party, which, under God, has so far saved the country from hopeless ruin. As President Of the United States, your official act which first startled your friends in Indiana and caused them TO pause, was your veto Of the Civil Rights Bill. As I read and re-read your annual message to my mind there clearly traceable and ably affirmed IN that document, every important principle contained in the Civil Rights Bill. Next IN the category of this stifling and stunning process was your anomalous and inexplicable course in opposition to the finally mild and conservative action Of Congress—precedent TO the admission of representatives from States lately in armed rebellion against the Government. Did it occur to you in the incipiency of your opposition that in that action Of Congress every member of the most numerous branch of that body who voted to elevate you to the Vice Presidency in 1861 also voted for the late proposed amendments to the Federal Constitution? This much your friends felt you owed both TO the memories of the heroic dead and TO the interests present and future Of our distracted country.

Jackson, of Indiana, graduate of Asbury Univ., a very model man, sent by the authorities of the Methodist Episcopal Church to preach the Gospel IN the city of New Orleans. He was first knocked down and shamefully beaten, then shot through the body, the ball passing through both lungs, and others doubtless nonoffensive fell victims to violence on that dreadful day. By whose hands was this foul and fearful work accomplished? Answer not by the loyal Union-loving men who elevated you TO power, and who followed the old flag through the dark hours of war, but by those who for four long years were in armed rebellion against the Government, who still hate it in their hearts and who once hated You with equal malignity, but who now, for some reason, amid the wild carnival of death, excite forward the infuriated mob by shouting "the President is on our side!
